task_row_model.query: In Python, how can I memoize a recursive function so it is safe to call from multiple threads and does not leak memory from per-key synchronization objects? Describe the minimal approach and key implementation steps.

documents.content: Academic note: Memoization stores previously computed results to avoid recomputation; a bounded LRU cache limits memory growth and is preferred over an unbounded dict for long-running services. For recursive functions, a cache must return results for previously computed inputs to short-circuit deeper recursion. Standard library decorators provide bounded caches, but concurrency introduces races: two threads might both observe a cache miss and compute the same key simultaneously. Therefore, beyond choosing a bounded cache, explicit synchronization is required to serialize computation per key or to coordinate in-progress computations so only one thread does the work and others wait for the result.
documents.reasoning_trace: Included LRU/bounded cache rationale and noted that concurrency requires extra synchronization to prevent duplicate work.

documents.content: Tech article: In multi-threaded code the classic problem is the duplicate-computation race: thread A and thread B both check the cache, see a miss, and compute the same expensive value. Two pragmatic patterns avoid this: (1) per-key locks – a lock is associated with each cache key so only one thread computes that key at a time; (2) in-progress placeholders like futures/promises – the first thread inserts a placeholder representing the ongoing computation and others await its completion. Both require a double-checked pattern: check cache, if missing create/get synchronization object atomically, acquire or await it, then re-check the cache before computing and finally store the result and signal completion.
documents.reasoning_trace: Described per-key lock and future/placeholder patterns plus double-checked locking to avoid races.

documents.content: Reference entry / informal note: Storing a Lock object for every observed key can itself leak memory if keys are numerous and never removed. Use a weak-value mapping (weakref.WeakValueDictionary) for per-key locks or placeholders so the lock object can be garbage-collected when no longer referenced elsewhere. The pattern: have a bounded result cache and a weak-value dict of locks/futures; when handling a key, get or create its synchronization object from the weak dict, acquire or await it, perform computation if still missing, write back to the bounded cache, and release/signal. This keeps per-key synchronization ephemeral and avoids unbounded growth of the lock table.
documents.reasoning_trace: Added weakref.WeakValueDictionary advice to prevent lock-table memory leaks and tied it to the bounded cache pattern.

documents.content: Background/history and definitions: Memoization emerged from functional-programming practices in the 1960s as a way to trade space for time; dynamic programming formalized similar reuse of subproblem solutions. Some tutorials repeat definitions of time/space tradeoffs and present Fibonacci as the canonical example. Occasional blog posts throw in broad statistics about cache hit rates in web services, unrelated case studies about database caching, and long-winded comparisons to hardware caching. These tangential discussions are useful for context but do not affect the core implementation choices for thread-safe, bounded memoization.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Use a bounded LRU result cache to prevent unbounded memory growth. To make memoization thread-safe and avoid duplicate work, use a per-key synchronization object (lock or future) and the double-checked pattern: check cache, if missing get-or-create the per-key lock/future, acquire/await it, re-check cache, compute and store result, then release/signal. Keep per-key synchronization objects in a weakref.WeakValueDictionary so the lock table does not leak memory.
